text.text: Schistosomiasis remains a major public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa.

Recent World Health Organization (WHO) guidance calls for community-wide treatment and fine-scale data to optimise preventive chemotherapy (PC) strategies, yet the practical implications for resource allocation by health ministries are unclear.
We analysed epidemiological and cost data from Ethiopia and Zimbabwe to compare survey designs and five implementation scenarios.
Scenarios varied by data source, administrative unit of implementation, and WHO guidance on PC strategies.
Outcomes were target population, praziquantel requirements, and delivery costs.
The geostatistical approach reduced sample size by up to 90% and survey costs by ≥72% compared with a design-based approach, while increasing spatial coverage.
Applying updated WHO guidance expanded eligibility to pre-school-aged children and adults, and in one scenario increased treatment eligibility by 72% in Ethiopia and 262% in Zimbabwe.
Correspondingly, praziquantel requirements and delivery costs were driven primarily by expanded age eligibility rather than geographic coverage.
The geostatistical approach provides substantial efficiency gains for impact assessments, enabling costefficient, granular targeting.

However, implementing 2022 WHO guidance was the dominant driver of increases in programme scope and resource needs, underscoring the importance of accurate fine-scale data to guide efficient planning and budgeting toward elimination goals.
Schistosomiasis continues to pose a major public health problem in the African region [1].

text.text: The geostatistical approach for both design and analysis was selected by the health ministries due to its sampling efficiency, whilst ensuring statistical rigour, as compared to design-based cluster surveys [11, 22].
text.formatted: The geostatistical approach for both design and analysis was selected by the health ministries due to its sampling efficiency, whilst ensuring statistical rigour, as compared to design-based cluster surveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">22]</ref>.

text.text: The geostatistical approach to impact assessments provided the Ethiopian and Zimbabwean health ministries with precise prevalence classifications at the sub-IU (kebele and ward, respectively).
Impact assessment data were then used to support decisions on which populations to target with priority interventions, including PC.

At the time of conducting the data collection surveys in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe (2019-24), existing WHO algorithms were in place to support post-impact assessment decision-making for PC frequency and target populations for schistosomiasis [8].
text.formatted: At the time of conducting the data collection surveys in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe (2019-24), existing WHO algorithms were in place to support post-impact assessment decision-making for PC frequency and target populations for schistosomiasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[8]</ref>.

text.text: During the period of impact assessment analysis (2022-23), new WHO guidelines were released which updated the PC decision-making thresholds and algorithms [6].
text.formatted: During the period of impact assessment analysis (2022-23), new WHO guidelines were released which updated the PC decision-making thresholds and algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The new guidelines included widening the target population from school-aged children (SAC) and at-risk adults in high prevalence areas to whole communities from two years of age and lowering the prevalence threshold for this community-wide treatment to 10% prevalence, from 50%, for annual PC with PZQ.

With these simultaneous changes to decision-making rules and requirements for more precise epidemiological data, we hypothesised that (1) a geostatistical approach would reduce sample size and survey cost, relative to a design-based survey, while improving spatial targeting; (2) moving decision-making from the IU to the sub-IU would allow PC to be reduced or increased in more focal areas, reducing the geographic extent of annual PC; and (3) the 2022 WHO guidelines would show an expansion in the total population eligible for PC and hence PZQ requirements and delivery cost, offsetting any geographic shrinkage of need.

This study aimed to use epidemiological and cost evidence from Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, to demonstrate efficiency gains in survey design and to determine differences in target populations and costs when using (i) more precise epidemiological data from impact assessments, (ii) historical and updated WHO guidelines, and (iii) IU versus sub-IU as a unit for informing intervention decisions.

These results increase the evidence in understanding optimal survey designs and resource allocation and are the first to demonstrate the impact of policy changes in the implementation of national control and elimination programmes for schistosomiasis in sub-Saharan Africa.

Historically, Ethiopia and Zimbabwe health ministry programmes have implemented at the IU-level, which is woreda and district, respectively and shifted to sub-IU schistosomiasis PC, targeting kebele and ward based on recent prevalence data.

The geostatistical models underpinning the sub-IU prevalence classifications were developed, validated and reported as part of the respective national impact assessments [23, 24]; they were not re-estimated for this study.

The analyses presented here take the published sub-IU prevalence classifications as fixed inputs and apply WHO decision algorithms and programme cost data to them.

All data were shared with the research team for the purposes of this study.

Impact assessments were costed as surveys using either a design-based cluster approach, which was not conducted and is costed here as a hypothetical comparator, or the geostatistical approach that was implemented.

text.text: Costs were estimated assuming several parameters.
Sample sizes for the design-based survey assumed 30 SAC per site with five sites randomly selected per suspected or known endemic sub-IU.
Sub-IUs not suspected or known to be endemic were not sampled and were classified as non-endemic.
In the designbased survey analysis, inaccessible areas due to insecurity and political instability were excluded from the sub-IU estimates in Ethiopia.

The design-based parameters were set to a 95% confidence interval, 85% power, a 10% margin of error, and an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.10 to provide a precise estimate of sub-IU prevalence following the parameters derived by Knowles et al. for cluster surveys designed to plan schistosomiasis PC [25].

Across two national programmes, we found that using a geostatistical approach for schistosomiasis impact assessments delivered sub-IU prevalence estimates with far lower survey effort and cost than a design-based approach, while increasing spatial coverage of data for programmatic decision-making.
When those sub-IU data were paired with the 2022 WHO guidelines, the population eligible for PC, PZQ needs, and delivery costs rose substantially.
These increased resources were driven mainly by the inclusion of adults and pre-SAC rather than by expansion of the number of areas treated.
Our first and third hypotheses were supported.

The second was not, moving decisions from the IU to the sub-IU changed the number of sub-IUs requiring PC by less than 3% in either country (Scenario Three); the reduction in geographic extent came instead from the change in guidance (Scenario Four).

In brief, measurement efficiency through a geostatistical approach reduces survey inputs, and increases decision efficiency through sub-IU targeting, but eligibility expansion is the dominant driver of programme scale.

text.text: Several caveats merit consideration.

The geostatistical approach relies on spatial interpolation; prediction uncertainty increases in data-sparse areas, and conservative exclusion rules may bias some estimates downward in inaccessible locations.

Cost estimates reflect financial delivery costs and do not include all economic inputs (e.g., training, supervision, infrastructure, health system strengthening, opportunity costs, MoH overheads), thus underestimating the true costs.

WorldPop population estimates are subject to uncertainty, particularly in remote areas or rapidly changing populations, which may affect estimates of the population requiring preventive chemotherapy and programme costs.
Scenario analyses applied WHO algorithms consistently and did not simulate country-specific deviations, phased rollouts, or supply-chain constraints; thus, implementation realities may differ.
These findings may be relevant to other schistosomiasis-endemic countries undertaking impact assessments and adopting the 2022 WHO guidelines as they transition towards elimination.

How much the eligible population increases is likely to depend on the size of the already-treated population relative to the total population in areas meeting the treatment threshold: in Ethiopia, where a large school-based programme was already established, the eligible population rose by 72%, whereas in Zimbabwe, where a proportionally smaller population was being treated, it rose by 262%.

However, the magnitude of these effects will vary according to local epidemiology, health system capacity, and programme delivery structures, and generalisability should be tested further before policy adoption.

Finally, limited institutional capacity in geostatistics constrains scale-up, and complex or uncertain model outputs can be hard for non-specialists to interpret-delaying decisions-so building capacity, increasing modelling transparency, and engaging stakeholders are essential to improve uptake.
The findings are also conditional on the assumptions applied.

Where the 2011 guidance specifies "maintain previous frequency" without a frequency, we applied annual PC; a less intensive interpretation would reduce the population attributed to the 2011 guidance and therefore increase, rather than decrease, the expansion we attribute to the 2022 guidance.

The interpretations applied to the WHO algorithms follow WHO/ESPEN's CDAT [34], although countries may deviate from these at verification, and the rule aggregating sub-IU classifications to IU level is a programmatic choice, so alternative thresholds would alter the IU-level scenarios though not Scenarios Four and Five.

The survey cost comparison is insensitive to unit costs because both survey types were costed from the same unit costs, so an error in any price affects both approaches and largely cancels; the exception is technical support, which is higher for the geostatistical approach and therefore narrows the reported difference (Supplementary Table S2).

text.text: These results identify two complementary aspects for improving programme efficiency and impact.

First, measurement: a geostatistical approach provides precise, cost-effective data that supports decision-making and allows resources to shift from data collection to delivery without compromising accuracy.
Second, implementation: moving treatment decisions from IU to sub-IU improves treatment efficiency by allowing more granular, evidence-based targeting that accounts for spatial heterogeneity.

In our scenarios, this refinement increased the population requiring PC, though less than the effect of the WHO guidance, by identifying persistent or emerging hotspots previously masked by IU-level aggregated prevalence.
This approach is likely to be embedded in ESPEN microplanning tools which integrate historical epidemiological data, environmental suitability, and local knowledge [34, 42].

text.text: Since the 2022 WHO guidance expands eligibility beyond SAC, national drug needs and delivery budgets may rise even if the number of areas treated remains stable or declines, particularly due to adult inclusion..

This study does not fully consider the additional health system capacity that may be required to support expanded treatment eligibility, including workforce, supply chains, monitoring systems, and community engagement.

Therefore, future operational research evaluating the real-world implementation, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and long-term sustainability of these recommendations in different endemic settings would further knowledge on efficiency gains for schistosomiasis treatment programmes.
The geostatistical approach provides a cost-efficient route for generating the fine-scale evidence required for programme decision-making.
Implementation of the 2022 WHO guideline at the sub-IU level substantially expands treatment eligibility, primarily because of changes in eligibility criteria rather than geographic expansion.

Countries planning for elimination as a public health problem should pair efficient measurement with granular implementation and realistic budgeting for expanded eligibility to maximise health impact and avoid systematic under-treatment.

Realising these gains depends on two conditions that not all programmes currently meet: access to epidemiological data of sufficient quality and spatial resolution to support sub-IU decisions, and the implementation capacity to deliver treatment at that resolution.

Despite the reduction in geographic spread, the population requiring PC approximately doubled across both contexts, rising from 8.94 to 17.06 million (90.8%) in Ethiopia, and from 3.05 to 6.34 million (107.9%) in Zimbabwe. Adults, previously treated only under specific criteria, became eligible under 2022 guidelines, increasing by 10.78 million across both countries. Pre-SAC who were also previously ineligible, increased by 3.03 million in total. In both countries, a reduction in the number of SAC requiring PC fell alongside the geographic spread owing to the reduction in PC frequency from biennial to triennial (Tables 1, 5). Scenario Five. Effect of a change in all decision-variables: epidemiological data, administrative unit plus WHO guidelines Scenario Five changes all three decision-variables: data source, administrative unit and WHO guidance, the last including a lower prevalence threshold for treating adults and the addition of pre-SAC. This resulted in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe experiencing large increases in people requiring PC (Table 4).

In Ethiopia, sub-IUs meeting the treatment threshold fell by 42.5% (7,902 to 4,544), while the population requiring PC rose from 9.92 to 17.06 million (72.0%). Pre-SAC and adults requiring treatment expanded, but by comparison, SAC targets declined by 22.6% (9.01 to 6.97 million), consistent with reduced transmission in historically treated age groups.

In Zimbabwe, the number of sub-IUs requiring PC changed marginally (1,569 to 1,723; 9.8%). Pre-SAC and adults requiring treatment increased, while SAC requiring PC rose more modestly (1.66 to 2.55 million, 53.6%). bib.title: Despite the reduction in geographic spread, the population requiring PC approximately doubled across both contexts, rising from 8.94 to 17.06 million (90.8%) in Ethiopia, and from 3.05 to 6.34 million (107.9%) in Zimbabwe. Adults, previously treated only under specific criteria, became eligible under 2022 guidelines, increasing by 10.78 million across both countries. Pre-SAC who were also previously ineligible, increased by 3.03 million in total. In both countries, a reduction in the number of SAC requiring PC fell alongside the geographic spread owing to the reduction in PC frequency from biennial to triennial (Tables 1, 5). Scenario Five.
